title: SHE SHARED HIS BED… BUT NEVER HELD THE TITLE OF WIFE. WHY DID THE OLD TESTAMENT ALLOW THIS?
paragraphs: SHE SHARED HIS BED… BUT NEVER HELD THE TITLE OF WIFE. WHY DID THE OLD TESTAMENT ALLOW THIS?
The disturbing truth about concubines, the women history often overlooked, and the God who never confused human permission with His perfect design.
There is a woman in the Bible whose story should make every Christian uncomfortable.
We do not know her name.
We do not know what she dreamed about when she was younger. We do not know whether she ever imagined being loved, protected, cherished, or growing old beside someone who would never abandon her.
But we know how her story ended.
Her body lay at the doorway of a house.
Her hands were stretched toward the threshold.
And the man who had been traveling with her said, “Up, and let us be going.”
There was no answer.
Judges 19:27–28.
Read those words again.
Because this was not a stranger.
She was his concubine.
And before you turn away from this disturbing passage, there is something you need to understand.
The Bible records things that God never approved.
Some of Scripture's darkest stories are not instructions for how God's people should live. They are warnings about what happens when human beings abandon His ways.
That distinction matters.
Because somewhere between the wives, the concubines, the kings, the patriarchs, and the laws of ancient Israel, a question emerges that Christians cannot afford to answer carelessly.
Why were concubines treated differently from wives in the Old Testament?
Did God consider some women less valuable than others?
Did having a concubine mean a man could enjoy the privileges of marriage without accepting its full responsibilities?
And if God created marriage between one man and one woman, why do we repeatedly encounter men in Scripture who had multiple wives and concubines?
The answer is not as simple as saying, “That was just their culture.”
Because culture explains some of what happened.
It does not automatically justify it.
And the deeper we go into Scripture, the more we discover something remarkable.
The Bible is not hiding the failures of its heroes. It is exposing humanity's desperate need for a Savior.
To understand concubinage, we must begin before Abraham, before Jacob, before David, and before Solomon.
We must return to a garden.
Before sin entered the world, there were no royal harems, no concubines competing for security, and no women being divided into categories according to their place within a man's household.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was a covenantal union established by God.
Genesis 2:24 declares:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” (KJV)
In the original Hebrew, the final expression is:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Ve-hayu le-vasar echad.
“And they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew word echad means “one.”
Here, the expression describes a profound union, not merely a physical encounter.
The man and woman are joined in a relationship that creates a new family bond.
Notice what the passage does not say.
It does not say a man shall accumulate women according to his wealth.
It does not establish one category of women for covenantal dignity and another for convenient companionship.
It presents a foundational picture of marriage.
One man.
One woman.
One flesh.
And when Jesus later addressed marriage in Matthew 19:4–6, He returned to this very beginning.
Not to Solomon's palace.
Not to Jacob's household.
Not to the customs of ancient kings.
To creation.
That is significant.
Because when Jesus wanted to explain God's intention for marriage, He pointed His listeners back to what God established before human rebellion distorted relationships.
But the world outside Eden was different.
Sin entered.
Power became corrupted.
Human relationships became tangled in pride, jealousy, exploitation, insecurity, and the desire to control.
And eventually, Scripture introduces a man named Lamech.
Genesis 4:19 records that Lamech took two wives.
The Bible does not pause to celebrate his decision.
It simply records it.
That is one of the most important principles for interpreting Old Testament narratives:
Description is not the same as divine endorsement.
Just because a biblical character did something does not mean God commanded it, celebrated it, or intended everyone else to imitate it.
Abraham lied.
Jacob deceived.
David committed adultery and arranged a man's death.
Solomon pursued relationships that turned his heart away from the Lord.
Their inclusion in Scripture does not make their sins holy.
It demonstrates how deeply humanity needs grace.
And this brings us to the concubines.
In the Hebrew Bible, one of the primary words translated “concubine” is:
פִּילֶגֶשׁ
Pilegesh.
The precise historical origin of this Hebrew word is uncertain, but its biblical usage generally identifies a woman in a recognized secondary marital or household relationship.
A concubine was not simply the ancient equivalent of a modern girlfriend.
Nor was she necessarily a prostitute or a woman involved in a casual relationship.
Concubinage was a socially recognized institution in parts of the ancient Near East.
A concubine could belong to a man's household, bear his children, and have a continuing relationship with him.
But her status was generally lower than that of a principal wife.
The exact legal arrangements varied across periods, regions, and households.
And that last detail is important.
The Old Testament does not present one comprehensive, uniform legal definition governing every concubine in every generation.
Sometimes a concubine had previously been enslaved.
Sometimes she was connected to a household through a secondary union.
Sometimes her position was closely tied to inheritance, family arrangements, or royal power.
And sometimes the Bible uses marital language in ways that overlap with the language of concubinage.
For example, Genesis 25:1 calls Keturah Abraham's wife, while 1 Chronicles 1:32 identifies her as Abraham's concubine.
This reminds us that ancient household categories cannot always be forced neatly into modern definitions.
Nevertheless, a broad distinction remains.
A principal wife generally occupied a more established and socially prominent marital position.
A concubine generally held a secondary position, often with fewer recognized privileges and less security.
Her children could be acknowledged as the father's children, but their inheritance prospects might differ.
Genesis 25:5–6 gives us a striking example.
Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac, while also giving gifts to the sons of his concubines and sending them away from Isaac.
The passage demonstrates a real distinction in inheritance arrangements.
But it does not prove that every concubine's child was automatically excluded from every inheritance in ancient Israel.
The circumstances varied.
And here is where the question becomes painfully human.
Imagine living in a household where your security depended heavily on the favor of a powerful man.
Imagine bearing children who might never enjoy the same position as another woman's children.
Imagine knowing you belonged to the family, yet not possessing the same standing within it.
Now imagine being told that because this arrangement appears in the Bible, God must have considered it ideal.
That would be a serious misunderstanding of Scripture.
Because God's willingness to deal with people inside a broken social system does not mean He created that brokenness or approved every part of it.
Consider Hagar.
Her story begins in Genesis 16.
She was an Egyptian servant belonging to Sarai, Abraham's wife.
God had promised Abraham descendants.
But the years passed.
The waiting became painful.
And Sarai decided to take matters into her own hands.
She gave Hagar to Abraham.
Genesis 16:3 says Sarai gave Hagar to Abram “to be his wife” (KJV).
Yet Hagar's position remained deeply unequal.
She was still a servant.
She did not suddenly gain Sarai's authority.
And when Hagar conceived, conflict erupted.
Sarai treated her harshly.
Hagar fled.
Think about that.
A woman was drawn into a family arrangement shaped by someone else's desperation.
She became pregnant.
Then she found herself running into the wilderness.
And there, far from the security of the household, the angel of the LORD encountered her.
Genesis 16:13 records Hagar's response:
“Thou God seest me.” (KJV)
In Hebrew, the passage includes the expression:
אֵל רֳאִי
El Ro'i.
Commonly understood as “God who sees me,” though the precise rendering of the expression is discussed by translators.
The meaning within the story is extraordinary.
Hagar had been overlooked by powerful people.
But she had not escaped God's attention.
She was a servant.
A foreigner.
A woman whose life had become entangled in the failures of Abraham and Sarai.
Yet God addressed her personally.
He heard her suffering.
He spoke concerning her son.
And later, when Hagar and Ishmael were sent away, God again heard the boy and provided for them in the wilderness (Genesis 21:17–19).
Do not misunderstand this.
God's care for Hagar does not mean He approved every decision that brought her into that situation.
Nor does His command to her in Genesis 16:9 erase the hardship or moral complexity of her circumstances.
But the narrative makes something unmistakable.
Hagar's social status did not determine whether God would see her.
And perhaps someone reading this knows what it feels like to be treated as secondary.
Not necessarily as a concubine.
But as an afterthought.
The person contacted only when someone needs something.
The spouse who gives everything yet feels invisible.
The child who grew up wondering why another sibling received more affection.
The believer who smiles in church while quietly carrying the wound of being unwanted.
People may rank human beings according to usefulness, wealth, beauty, reputation, or status.
But Scripture repeatedly confronts the arrogance of treating another person as though their dignity depends on human approval.
Genesis 1:27 establishes that humanity was created in God's image.
That truth is older than every royal household and every ancient inheritance custom.
And it belongs to women as surely as it belongs to men.
Now consider Jacob.
He loved Rachel.
But through Laban's deception, he first married Leah.
Then he married Rachel.
And eventually, the household included Bilhah and Zilpah, the servants of Rachel and Leah, who bore children to Jacob.
Genesis 30 records these arrangements.
Genesis 35:22 explicitly identifies Bilhah as Jacob's concubine.
But what does this household reveal?
Peace?
Contentment?
A beautiful example of covenantal harmony?
No.
It reveals rivalry.
Jealousy.
Pain.
Competition.
A desperate struggle for love and recognition.
Leah longed for Jacob's affection.
Rachel struggled with infertility.
Children became entangled in the emotional conflicts of adults.
And the household that would produce the twelve tribes of Israel was far from an example of perfect family relationships.
Yet God continued working through this deeply imperfect family.
That is grace.
But grace must never be confused with approval.
God's faithfulness to His promises does not mean every human decision within the story was righteous.
Sometimes the Bible shows us God accomplishing His purposes despite people's failures, not because those failures were good.
And then we arrive at the laws of Moses.
This is where some readers become confused.
Because the Law contains provisions addressing relationships involving enslaved women, multiple wives, and unequal household arrangements.
Exodus 21:7–11, for example, deals with a female servant in circumstances involving marriage arrangements.
The passage places obligations on the household and addresses her rights if certain provisions are not fulfilled.
Exodus 21:10 specifically mentions food, clothing, and marital rights in a situation where a man takes another wife.
Deuteronomy 21:15–17 addresses inheritance when a man has two wives and favors one over the other.
These passages show that the Law sometimes regulated social situations that already existed.
But regulating an existing practice is not necessarily the same as declaring it God's highest ideal.
Jesus Himself provides an important interpretive principle in Matthew 19:8.
Speaking about divorce, He says:
“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.” (KJV)
Jesus was speaking specifically about divorce.
We should not pretend that this statement directly explains every law concerning concubines.
Nevertheless, it demonstrates that Scripture itself distinguishes between certain accommodations within a fallen society and God's intention from creation.
This is why we must read the Old Testament carefully.
We cannot simply collect everything that happened under the old covenant and announce that every recorded arrangement represents God's timeless moral ideal.
And we cannot ignore the protective intent of certain laws merely because the social world they addressed was deeply unequal.
The Law sometimes restrained harm within conditions that were far from Eden.
But the presence of regulation did not magically transform every unequal relationship into a model for Christian marriage.
In fact, the Old Testament itself repeatedly exposes the dangers of multiplying wives.
Deuteronomy 17:17 warns Israel's future king:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.” (KJV)
Now think about Solomon.
A man associated with extraordinary wisdom.
A king who possessed wealth, influence, power, and international prestige.
Yet 1 Kings 11:3 records that he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines.
One thousand women.
And Scripture does not describe this as the triumph of biblical masculinity.
It tells us that his wives turned away his heart.
The man who possessed extraordinary wisdom still failed to guard his devotion to God.
That should humble every believer.
Because knowledge of God is not the same as obedience to God.
Religious privilege is not the same as faithfulness.
And having access to Scripture does not mean someone is automatically living according to it.
Solomon's relationships were not merely private romantic arrangements.
Royal marriages could involve political alliances, wealth, succession, and power.
Concubines in royal households could also be connected to the public demonstration of a king's status and authority.
That helps explain why royal concubines sometimes appear in political conflicts.
In 2 Samuel 16:21–22, Absalom publicly took his father's concubines in an act connected to his rebellion against David.
The women were caught in a violent struggle for royal power.
Then 2 Samuel 20:3 tells us David provided for the ten concubines involved but did not resume sexual relations with them. They remained confined to a form of widowhood while he was still alive.
Pause there.
These women were not merely symbols in a political drama.
They were human beings whose lives were permanently affected by the actions of powerful men.
The text does not tell us everything they thought or felt.
We must not invent details Scripture does not provide.
But it tells us enough to recognize the tragic consequences of a household system in which women's lives could become entangled with royal ambition.
And then there is the unnamed concubine in Judges 19.
One of the most horrifying accounts in the Old Testament.
The woman is sexually assaulted by a mob after being handed over to them.
The next morning, she is found at the doorway.
Her death is strongly implied by the narrative, and Judges 20:5 later reports that she died.
Her body is subsequently dismembered and sent throughout Israel.
There is no responsible way to turn this passage into comfortable religious entertainment.
The account is meant to horrify us.
And the wider book of Judges repeatedly describes a society collapsing into moral chaos.
Judges 21:25 concludes:
“In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.” (KJV)
The repeated refrain exposes the disorder of Israel's life in that period.
But we should also be careful not to reduce this woman's suffering to a simple illustration about political leadership.
The narrative exposes violence, failed protection, collective wickedness, and profound moral breakdown.
And it forces us to confront a difficult reality.
A society can possess religious language and still become terrifyingly cruel to vulnerable people.
The existence of a biblical covenant community did not mean everyone within it acted faithfully.
The existence of religious customs did not mean women were always treated justly.
And the existence of a man with social authority did not make his decisions righteous.
If anything, this story should make us more serious about protecting the vulnerable, condemning sexual violence, and refusing to use Scripture to excuse abuse.
Because no woman becomes less human because she lacks social power.
No person becomes disposable because another person has greater authority.
And no amount of religious language can transform cruelty into holiness.
Perhaps this is where the question becomes even more personal.
Because we live in a different century, but human hearts have not changed nearly as much as we imagine.
We may no longer use the word pilegesh in ordinary conversation.
But we still see people wanting the benefits of intimacy without accepting the responsibilities of faithful love.
We still see relationships built on unequal power.
We still see people treated as replaceable.
We still see men and women wounded by promises that were never meant to be kept.
We still see people using religious language to defend selfish desires.
And we still see wounded souls wondering whether God notices what others have done to them.
That is why this subject matters.
It is not merely an ancient historical curiosity.
It exposes questions about power, commitment, dignity, justice, and the human tendency to turn another person into something useful rather than someone to love.
But the Bible does not end with the failures of patriarchs and kings.
It moves toward Jesus Christ.
And when Jesus enters the story, something remarkable happens.
He does not treat women as spiritually insignificant.
He speaks with the Samaritan woman at the well in John 4.
He receives the devotion of Mary, who sits at His feet as a disciple in Luke 10:38–42.
He defends the woman who anoints Him in Luke 7:36–50.
He heals women, listens to them, and receives them among His followers.
And when Mary Magdalene encounters the risen Christ, John 20 records her role in announcing His resurrection to the disciples.
These encounters do not mean that every social injustice instantly disappeared from the ancient world.
They reveal the character of the Savior.
Jesus does not measure a person's worth by the social hierarchy that surrounds them.
He calls people to repentance.
He extends mercy.
He confronts hypocrisy.
He restores dignity.
And He reveals what love looks like when it is not corrupted by the desire to dominate.
Consider what Paul later writes in Ephesians 5:25:
In the Greek text, the command begins:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas.
“Husbands, love your wives.”
The verb agapate comes from agapaō, meaning “to love.”
The passage does not leave the meaning of that love to a husband's selfish imagination.
It provides a model.
Christ.
And what did Christ do?
He gave Himself.
He sacrificed.
He did not exploit His bride.
He did not abandon her when loving her became costly.
He gave Himself for her good.
That is the standard Paul places before Christian husbands.
Not Solomon's accumulation of women.
Not the competition inside Jacob's household.
Not the political arrangements of ancient kings.
Christ's sacrificial love.
And this is where the entire discussion changes.
Because the ultimate Christian model for marriage is not the most powerful man in the Old Testament.
It is Jesus Christ.
The One who loved sacrificially.
The One who remained faithful.
The One who laid down His life.
The One whose love cannot be purchased with beauty, status, wealth, or social influence.
The One who came to redeem sinners rather than use them.
Now, we must be careful.
Jesus did not come merely to provide a better example of human relationships.
He came to save sinners.
The deepest problem in humanity is not simply that people have constructed unjust social arrangements.
It is that sin has corrupted our relationship with God and with one another.
We have rebelled against our Creator.
We have pursued selfish desires.
We have harmed others.
We have failed to love as we should.
And none of us can make ourselves righteous by comparing our behavior with someone else's failures.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” (KJV)
That includes kings.
Patriarchs.
Religious leaders.
Husbands.
Wives.
And every person reading these words.
But the Gospel does not leave us under condemnation without hope.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
There it is.
The difference between human exploitation and divine redemption.
Sinful humanity often asks, “What can I get from this person?”
Christ demonstrated a love that gave Himself to rescue those who could never earn their salvation.
At the cross, Jesus bore the penalty of sin.
Through His resurrection, He conquered death.
And through repentance and faith in Him, sinners receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
This is not permission to continue harming others.
Grace does not excuse cruelty.
Forgiveness does not erase the need for repentance.
And Christian love never requires victims to remain in dangerous or abusive situations.
The Gospel calls those who have sinned to turn from their sin.
It calls those who have abused power to abandon exploitation and accept responsibility.
It calls believers to pursue holiness, justice, mercy, and truth.
And it reminds the wounded that another person's wrongdoing does not determine their worth before God.
Maybe you have never thought much about concubines before today.
Maybe the subject sounded strange, uncomfortable, or irrelevant.
But perhaps you kept reading because something deeper began to stir.
Perhaps you recognized the pain of being treated as less important.
Perhaps you remembered a relationship where someone wanted your loyalty but refused to give you theirs.
Perhaps you have watched someone misuse the Bible to justify behavior that contradicted the character of Christ.
Or perhaps you are confronting something in your own heart.
A tendency to control.
A desire to be served without serving.
A willingness to excuse selfishness because someone in Scripture once behaved similarly.
If that is you, do not run from conviction.
Bring it to Jesus.
There is forgiveness for the repentant.
There is grace for the humbled.
There is healing for the wounded.
There is transformation for those who surrender to Christ.
And there is a better way to love.
Not because human beings suddenly become perfect.
But because the Holy Spirit works in those who belong to Jesus, teaching them to turn away from sin and walk in obedience.
The story of concubines in the Old Testament is therefore not a story about God creating different grades of human worth.
It is a story unfolding within ancient societies where marriage, slavery, inheritance, fertility, political power, and household status were often deeply intertwined.
Some concubines occupied recognized secondary marital positions.
Some were enslaved women whose choices were severely constrained.
Some bore children who became important figures in Israel's history.
Some suffered profoundly.
And Scripture does not portray every such relationship in exactly the same way.
We should resist both extremes.
We must not claim that every concubine was identical to a modern sex slave, because the historical evidence does not support such a sweeping statement.
But neither should we romanticize concubinage as though unequal status, constrained freedom, and diminished security were unimportant.
The biblical accounts demand more honesty than either simplification allows.

And when we ask why concubines were treated differently from wives, the historical answer is that ancient household systems distinguished between principal and secondary unions, with differences in status, legal protection, social recognition, and sometimes inheritance.
The theological answer requires us to go further.
Those distinctions arose within human societies marked by sin and inequality.
They were not a declaration that women possessed different levels of value before their Creator.
The Bible's larger story moves from God's good creation, through humanity's rebellion, toward redemption in Jesus Christ and the promised restoration of all things.
That is why we must never build our understanding of God's heart on an isolated ancient custom while ignoring the whole counsel of Scripture.
And that is why we must never use the failures of biblical figures as permission to repeat them.
Abraham needed grace.
Jacob needed grace.
David needed grace.
Solomon needed grace.
And we need grace too.
Not cheap grace that tells us our sins do not matter.
But the costly grace purchased through the blood of Jesus Christ.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that confronts.
Grace that restores.
Grace that transforms.
Grace that teaches us to love people as people, not possessions.
If this article has exposed something you have struggled to understand, I want to invite you into the conversation.
You do not have to pretend that every passage is easy.
Faithful Bible study makes room for difficult questions while remaining committed to the truth of God's Word.
Not to reopen their pain.
But to remind them that the Lord sees what human beings overlook.
You never know which friend is silently questioning whether God cares about people who have been mistreated.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who have not yet come to faith in Jesus.
Because understanding the Bible should not be reserved for people who have already learned all the religious language.
The Word of God deserves to be opened, studied, understood, and shared.
And there is another way you can help this ministry continue.
It is not a requirement for glorifying God.
And it is not a replacement for the biblical responsibilities of generosity, worship, and care for your local church.
We never want financial pressure to replace cheerful generosity.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
These resources can serve as daily reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to share your faith.
The Library is a resource for spiritual nourishment and study, not a substitute for Scripture, prayer, fellowship, or faithful participation in a local church.
You can still help.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage a friend to open the Bible.
But Jesus Christ is the reason the mission exists.
And that distinction must never be forgotten.
Because one day, our lives will not be measured by how impressive our religious platforms became, how many followers we gained, or how much money we collected.
We will stand before the Lord who knows every heart.
The same Lord who saw Hagar in the wilderness.
The same Lord who condemned injustice through His prophets.
The same Lord who called sinners to repentance.
The same Lord who gave Himself on the cross.
The same Lord who rose again.
And the same Lord who is coming again.
So when you think about the concubines of the Old Testament, do not merely remember the complicated laws or the households of ancient kings.
Remember the human beings inside those stories.
Remember the difference between what Scripture records and what God commands.
Remember that no social title can increase or decrease the worth of someone created in God's image.
Remember that the sins of biblical heroes are not instructions for our lives.
And above all, remember Jesus.
Because the answer to humanity's brokenness is not found in defending every custom of the past.
It is found in surrendering to the Savior who came to redeem sinners and make all things new.
The world may remember the position someone gave you, but the God who saw Hagar in the wilderness knows your name—and no human rejection can erase the dignity He gave you.
